metadata.title: Cross-Country Estimates of Employment and Investment in Organisational Capital: A Task-Based Methodology Using the PIAAC Database
metadata.venue: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC background questionnaire information and then recalibrates survey weights to make the sample representative of aggregate and industry employment structures, following a methodology described in Squicciarini et al. (2015). The analytic steps include (i) constructing occupation-level OC task indices from PIAAC task-frequency responses, (ii) selecting OC-related occupations using distributional ranking and hierarchical clustering, and (iii) classifying respondents by whether they work in OC-related occupations to aggregate employment and earnings. For the employment/investment quantification, the authors explicitly state that survey weights are recalibrated and then used to compute total employment (including employees and self-employed) and employment by industry, firm size, and public/private sectors. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation via replicate designs is not documented here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not model cognitive achievement scores with plausible values; instead, it constructs OC-related occupation sets from PIAAC task-frequency responses and then aggregates employment and investment using labour force participation and earnings information. Because the dependent quantities are occupation-based employment/investment shares derived from survey responses and external benchmarks (e.g., OECD STAN value-added), PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript does not describe a specific missing-data strategy for PIAAC background questionnaire items used to compute task averages, so missing-data handling is not reported; this is a reporting gap for analysts who would need to reproduce the occupation-task indices.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses the first round of PIAAC (winter 2011–2012) and restricts to countries where occupational information is available at the 3-digit ISCO level; this yields 20 countries and 112 occupational categories. For each country and occupation, the authors compute average responses across 40 PIAAC task items (with a note that one task uses a different 5-point scale that is converted to a usable form). OC-related occupations are then selected using (a) a distribution-based top-quartile criterion based on the average and minimum responses across a chosen OC task bundle (main analysis uses 9 tasks), and (b) a hierarchical clustering approach using all tasks to form occupation clusters, with the top-quartile cluster cut-off. Finally, respondents are classified as employed in OC-related occupations versus not, and employment/investment aggregates are computed using recalibrated survey weights.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper develops a task-based methodology to measure employment and investment in organisational capital (OC) using the OECD PIAAC background questionnaire task-frequency information. It operationalises OC as firm-specific organisational knowledge reflected in workers’ performance of OC-relevant tasks, then identifies OC-related occupations via a distribution-based top-quartile rule (mainly using 9 OC tasks) combined with hierarchical clustering of occupations using the full task set. The study covers 20 countries (2011–2012 PIAAC round) and estimates OC employment shares and OC investment as 20% of wages for OC-related occupations, expressed relative to value-added from OECD STAN. Key descriptive results include an average OC employment share of 16% (9.5% Denmark to 26% UK) and an average OC investment share of 2.2% (1.4% Czech Republic to 3.7% UK). The paper does not report ML model performance metrics because it is not an ML prediction study; it also does not document a missing-data strategy for the task-frequency inputs, and the 20% capitalisation factor is an assumption not validated within the paper.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
